t: 3767 - Maximize Points After Choosing K Tasks
o:
Every task is worth max(t1[i], t2[i]) if there were no constraint, so start from that ideal total. The constraint forces at least k tasks onto technique 1. Tasks already favoring t1 incur no loss; tasks where t2 > t1 lose (t2 − t1) when switched. Hence, sort the losses of the unfavorable tasks ascending and absorb the k cheapest switches. If fewer than k tasks are unfavorable, the constraint is already satisfied for free.

Example 1: ideal = max(5,10)+max(2,3)+max(10,8) = 10+3+10 = 23; losses for tasks 0 and 1 are 5 and 1; switch the cheapest (loss 1) → 22. Example 2: all tasks favor t1, ideal 60 stands. Example 3: k=0, ideal 15 stands.
k: Switching task i from t2 to t1 costs exactly t2[i] − t1[i] when t2[i] > t1[i]
Pay the k smallest positive losses; greedy is optimal by an exchange argument

a.i: Compute the unconstrained optimum, collect positive deficits (t2−t1) for tasks where technique 2 wins, sort them, and subtract the k smallest. Any exchange of a chosen expensive switch for a cheaper one only improves the total, so the greedy is optimal.
s: total = Σ max(t1[i], t2[i]); losses = sorted [t2[i]−t1[i] for tasks with t2[i] > t1[i]]
Subtract the first min(k, len(losses)) losses from total
a.t: O(n log n) — collecting losses is O(n), sorting dominates

a.i: Instead of sorting all losses, keep a max-heap of the k smallest losses seen so far (or a running sum with a heap for eviction). This helps when k ≪ n, giving O(n log k).
s: Maintain a max-heap capped at k elements plus their sum
Push each positive loss; evict the largest when size exceeds k
Subtract the maintained sum from the baseline
a.t: O(n log k) — heap operations with capped size

w: Use the sort-based approach for clarity; the heap variant wins when k is tiny relative to n. Pitfalls: forgetting that switching more than k tasks is allowed but never beneficial (extra switches only lose points), and missing that tasks where t1 ≥ t2 should always use t1 (they satisfy the quota for free). Totals reach 1e10, so use 64-bit accumulators. Follow-up: exactly k tasks on technique 1, or a budget on total switches.
